title: Speaking practice: The Printing Press, a Wetland and a Fruit Survey
description: Eight speaking tasks: continue a story, respond to a number claim, explain a food chain with data, evaluate a town sign, explain a machine, argue about story characters, explain the printing press and present survey data.

stimuli.title: What happens next at the bus stop?
paragraphs: Imagine this scene from the beginning of a story. Amara stands at a bus stop in the rain. She is holding a small cardboard box. Inside the box is a tiny gray kitten that is shivering. The bus is turning the corner.
Your partner wants to hear the rest of the story. Tell what happens next.

stimuli.title: Which day was colder?
paragraphs: A weather chart shows the lowest temperature on two winter days.
Monday low: −3°C
Tuesday low: −7°C
Your classmate Dev says: “Negative seven is greater than negative three, because 7 is greater than 3. So Tuesday was warmer.”

stimuli.title: Herons, frogs, and insects in a wetland
paragraphs: Students studying a wetland were given sample yearly counts. Herons eat frogs, and frogs eat insects. You will explain the pattern to your science team.
Year 1: 12 herons, 300 frogs, 5,000 insects
Year 2: 25 herons, 180 frogs, 7,000 insects
Year 3: 30 herons, 90 frogs, 9,500 insects

stimuli.title: What should happen to the old train station?
paragraphs: The town of Oakfield has 100 families. A sign at the farmers market says: “Everyone in our town shops at the Saturday market!” The town asked each family a question last month. Here are the answers.
70 families shopped at the Saturday market last month.
30 families did not shop at the market.
Of those 30 families, 20 said Saturday is a workday for them.
You are speaking at the town meeting. Tell the council whether the sign is correct.

stimuli.title: Explain the library checkout machine
paragraphs: A new student wants to check out a book from the school library. The library has a self-checkout machine. A sign next to it shows these steps:
1. Tap your student card on the card reader.
2. Place the book flat under the scanner.
3. Wait for the green light and the beep.
4. Take the paper receipt. It shows the date the book is due.

stimuli.title: Mara or Ben: who chose better?
paragraphs: Your reading group read a short story and will discuss it. Here is the story summary.

Mara and Ben found a wallet in the schoolyard. Inside were $40 and an identification card. Mara said, “We could keep $10 as a reward and give the rest back. No one would know.” Ben said, “It is not ours. We should take it to the office with nothing missing.” Mara was quiet for a moment. Then she agreed. At the office, the secretary called the owner, a custodian who had been searching for his wallet all morning. He thanked them and said he had been saving the money for his daughter's school books.

stimuli.title: How the printing press changed communication
paragraphs: Your history class is studying the printing press. Your teacher gave you these notes and asked you to explain the changes to a small group.

Before the mid-1400s in Europe, books were copied by hand. One book could take months to copy, so books were rare and expensive. Around 1450, printers in Europe began using movable metal type and a press. A printer could make many copies of the same page quickly. Over the next decades, the price of books fell and more people learned to read. News, ideas, and scientific findings spread more quickly across Europe.

stimuli.title: Survey results: favorite lunch fruit
paragraphs: A class surveyed 30 students: “What is your favorite fruit at lunch?” Each student chose one fruit. The results are shown in this table.
Mango: 12 students
Apple: 9 students
Banana: 6 students
Orange: 3 students

items.stem: Tell your partner a short story about what happens next. Include the character, a problem, what the character does, and how the story ends.

checklist: I named the character and told what she wants or needs.
I told a problem.
I told what happens in order.
I told how the story ends.
exemplar: Continues the scene logically with a clear problem and resolution.
Tells events in order using sequence words.
Uses past tense for narration with mostly consistent control.
Adds descriptive details (the kitten, the rain, how Amara feels).
Ends the story with a clear conclusion.

support.clue: Think: What problem could Amara have with the kitten on the bus? Who could help her?
support.frame: Amara got on the bus, but ______. She felt ______. First, she ______. Then, ______. At last, ______. In the end, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different scene): “Daniel stood on the dock with a heavy bag. A boat was leaving. He ran, but the rope was already loose. First, he shouted to the captain. Then the captain turned the boat around. At last, Daniel jumped on. In the end, he sat down, smiling and out of breath.” Now continue Amara's story in the same way.

items.stem: Respond to Dev. Say whether you agree, and use a number line or a thermometer picture in your mind to explain which day was colder.

checklist: I said clearly whether I agree with Dev.
I told which number is greater, −3 or −7, and why.
I used a word such as colder, warmer, left, right, below, or above zero.
I gave a reason with because.
exemplar: States that Dev is not correct and that Tuesday was colder.
Explains that −7 is farther below zero (or farther left on the number line) than −3.
Correctly says −3 is greater than −7.
Uses comparison vocabulary (greater than, less than, colder, farther from zero in the negative direction).
Responds respectfully and directly to Dev's reasoning.

support.clue: Picture a thermometer. Which temperature is farther below zero? Where would −3 and −7 sit on a number line?
support.frame: I do not agree with Dev because ______. On a number line, −7 is to the ______ of −3. That means −3 is ______ than −7. So ______ was colder because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different comparison): “Mia says that a debt of $8 is better than a debt of $2 because 8 is greater than 2. I do not agree. Owing $8 means you are at −8 dollars, which is farther below zero than −2 dollars. So −2 is greater than −8, and the smaller debt is better.” Now answer Dev about the temperatures.

facts: On a number line, −7 is to the left of −3.

items.stem: Explain to your team how the change in the number of herons is connected to the change in frogs and insects. Use numbers from the counts and show the chain of cause and effect.

checklist: I described how the herons changed.
I connected the herons to the frogs, then the frogs to the insects.
I used numbers from at least two years.
I used cause-and-effect words such as because, so, and as a result.
exemplar: Identifies the trend in each population (herons up, frogs down, insects up).
Builds a chain: more herons eat more frogs; with fewer frogs, fewer insects are eaten.
Uses specific numbers from at least two years as evidence.
Uses cause-and-effect connectors accurately.
Uses terms such as population, predator, prey, increase, and decrease.

support.clue: Compare Year 1 and Year 3 for each animal. Then ask: who eats whom?
support.frame: From Year 1 to Year 3, the number of herons ______ from ___ to ___. Because herons eat ______, the number of frogs ______ from ___ to ___. As a result, fewer ______ were eaten, so the number of insects ______ from ___ to ___.
support.model: Mentor example (a different food chain): “When the number of owls went up, the number of mice went down because owls eat mice. As a result, fewer seeds were eaten by mice, so there were more plants growing in the field.” Now explain the chain of herons, frogs, and insects, and add numbers from the table.

facts: When a predator population grows, its prey population often decreases.
When the population of an animal that eats insects decreases, the number of insects can increase.

items.stem: Tell the council whether the market sign is correct. Give at least two reasons that use numbers from the survey.

checklist: I said whether the sign is correct.
I gave two reasons.
I used numbers from the survey.
I used a word such as should, because, or for example.
exemplar: States a clear position about the sign (it is not fully correct, because not every family shops at the market).
Gives at least two reasons that connect to the survey (70 of 100 families shopped; 30 did not; 20 of those 30 work on Saturday).
Uses persuasive or evaluating language (I think, for example, a better sentence).
May suggest a more accurate sentence, such as “Most families shop at the Saturday market.”
Speaks clearly with a beginning and a closing sentence.

support.clue: Look at how many families shopped and how many did not. Does the word “everyone” match those numbers? Think about a better word for the sign.
support.frame: I think the sign ______ correct because ______. In the survey, ___ families ______ and ___ families ______. Another reason is that ______. A better sentence for the sign is ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different sign): “I think the poster is not correct because it says nobody walks to school. In our count of 12 students, 3 walked and 9 came by bus. For example, three students came in together through the front gate. For these reasons, a better sentence is ‘Most students ride the bus.’” Now give your own position about the market sign.

facts: 70 out of 100 families is most, but not all, of the families.
20 of the 30 families who did not shop at the market said Saturday is a workday for them.

items.stem: Show the new student how to use the checkout machine. Explain the steps in order and tell why the receipt is important.

checklist: I explained all four steps.
I used order words such as first, next, then, and last.
I told what the receipt shows.
I used words that tell where things go, such as on, under, and next to.
exemplar: Explains all four steps in the correct order.
Uses sequence words and directive language (first, next, you should).
Uses location words accurately (tap on the reader, place under the scanner).
Explains that the receipt shows the due date and why that helps (to know when to return the book).
Speaks politely and clearly to a new student.

support.clue: The sign has four numbered steps. Say them in that order, and then look at step 4 for the answer about the receipt.
support.frame: First, you ______ your card on the ______. Next, you ______ the book ______ the scanner. Then, you wait for ______. Last, you take the ______. It is important because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different task): “First, you put your coins in the machine. Next, you press the button for the drink you want. Then, you wait for the drink to drop. Last, you take it from the slot at the bottom. It is important to take the change too, because it is your money.” Now explain the library machine in the same way.

items.stem: Argue which character's idea was better, Mara's or Ben's. Use at least two details from the story as evidence and explain what each detail shows.

checklist: I chose Mara's idea or Ben's idea.
I used at least two details from the story.
I explained what each detail shows about the characters or the problem.
I used a word such as because, since, or although.
exemplar: States a clear position about whose idea was better.
Uses at least two accurate story details (the $40 and the identification card, Mara agreeing, the custodian's search and his plan for the money).
Explains how each detail supports the position.
Compares the two ideas (keeping $10 versus returning everything).
Uses connectors for reasons or contrast (because, although, however).

support.clue: Think about what the custodian lost and what he needed the money for. Which idea respects that?
support.frame: I think ______'s idea was better because ______. In the story, ______. This shows that ______. Although ______, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story): “I think Rin's idea was better because she asked for help before climbing the tree. In the story, the branch was thin and cracked. This shows that Rin was thinking about safety. Although Dev's idea was faster, it could have hurt him.” Now argue about Mara's idea and Ben's idea with details from the wallet story.

items.stem: Explain how the printing press changed communication in Europe. Describe a chain of three causes and effects, and use connecting words to show how one change led to the next.

checklist: I described life before the printing press.
I explained three causes and effects in a chain.
I used connecting words such as because, as a result, therefore, and so.
I ended with a sentence about why the change mattered.
exemplar: Contrasts the situation before (hand-copied, rare, expensive books) with the situation after.
Builds a chain of three linked causes and effects (press makes copies quickly, books become cheaper, more people read, ideas spread faster).
Uses precise connectors of cause and result accurately.
Uses academic vocabulary such as movable type, copy, literacy, and spread.
Closes with a statement about the larger importance of the change.

support.clue: Find the sentence that says what the press could do. Then follow what happened to the price of books, to reading, and to ideas, one step at a time.
support.frame: Before the printing press, ______. Then printers began ______, so ______. Because ______, books became ______. As a result, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different change): “Before the telephone, people had to write letters to send news. Then telephone lines were built, so people could speak to each other from far away. Because messages arrived instantly, businesses could answer customers faster. As a result, cities grew more connected. Therefore, news traveled much faster than before.” Now explain the changes caused by the printing press in the same way.

facts: Before the mid-1400s in Europe, books were copied by hand.
Around 1450, movable-type printing presses began to be used in Europe.
Printing lowered the cost of books and increased the number of readers.
Printing helped ideas and news spread more quickly.

items.stem: Present the survey results to the class. Say which fruit is most popular and which is least popular, and use numbers to compare at least two pairs of fruits.

checklist: I said which fruit is most popular and which is least popular.
I used numbers from the table.
I compared two pairs of fruits, using words such as more than, fewer than, or times as many.
I gave a summary sentence.
exemplar: Correctly identifies mango (12) as most popular and orange (3) as least popular.
Makes accurate numerical comparisons (for example, mango has 3 more than apple, or 4 times as many students chose mango as orange).
Uses comparison vocabulary accurately (more than, fewer than, twice, times as many).
Organizes the talk: purpose, findings, summary.
Speaks clearly with correct number words.

support.clue: Look at the biggest number and the smallest number first. Then choose two fruits and subtract, or ask how many times larger one is.
support.frame: In this survey, ___ students answered. The most popular fruit is ______, with ___ students. The least popular fruit is ______, with ___. ______ has ___ more students than ______. Overall, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different survey): “In this survey, 20 students answered. The most popular sport is swimming, with 9 students. The least popular sport is tennis, with 2 students. Soccer had 5 students and running had 4. Swimming has 7 more students than tennis. Overall, swimming is the most popular sport.” Now present the fruit survey in the same way.

facts: Mango (12) is 3 more than apple (9), 6 more than banana (6), and 9 more than orange (3).
12 is 4 times 3; 9 is 3 times 3; 6 is 2 times 3.
